title: Most Australians labelled allergic to penicillin turn out not to be
body: On 22 October 2026 the Guardian reported that the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy had changed its penicillin allergy guidelines: about 2.8 million Australians, 1 in 10, have been labelled allergic, but up to 90% of them are not ([the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/22/penicillin-allergy-australia-doctors-antibiotic-guidelines)). Labels often come from a rash or nausea during an illness, which the illness may have caused, from doctors noting side effects as allergies to be safe, or from a childhood story. In a true allergy the body has made antibodies called IgE that sit on mast cells; a later dose links them and the cells release histamine within minutes, and US health officials say these antibodies may fade over time ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/antibiotic-use/hcp/clinical-signs/index.html)). A wrong label matters: penicillin is narrow, aimed at the bacteria behind an infection, while broader drugs used instead also kill helpful gut bacteria and leave room for drug-resistant superbugs. Doctors can check with a careful history, skin tests or, for low-risk patients, a dose given under watch; no one should test themselves.

slides.question: Of 10 Australians labelled allergic to penicillin, how many are probably not allergic at all?
slides.explanation: Up to 9 in 10, by the evidence behind the new guidelines of Australia’s allergy specialists (October 2026). About 2.8 million Australians carry the label.

slides.alt: Animation in clinic blue: an allergy tag, then 100 people, 10 tagged, 9 turning green. A rash during a fever; a tag kept from childhood. Gold antibodies on a lilac mast cell burst out pink histamine. A narrow drug clears coral bacteria; a broad one wipes out mint gut bacteria and violet move in.

slides.prompt: Treat patients labelled allergic to penicillin. Clear one patient’s infection while keeping at least 80% of their helpful gut bacteria.
slides.takeaway: Only checking the label first opens the way to penicillin, which in this toy model clears the infection and keeps 90% of the gut bacteria; the broader drug keeps 30% and feeds resistant ones.

slides.heading: How a true penicillin allergy works

steps.label: A first dose: the body makes antibodies
They sit on mast cells, ready
A later dose links the antibodies

left.label: Penicillin
left.text: Narrow: aimed at the kind of bacteria behind the infection, so more of the gut’s helpful bacteria survive.

right.label: Broader antibiotics
right.text: Also kill many helpful gut bacteria, leaving room for superbugs that resist many drugs.

slides.text: No one should try taking penicillin themselves to find out whether they are allergic. Antibiotics should only be taken when prescribed for the individual taking them.
slides.attribution: Nick Cooling, Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

slides.question: Why can a wrong penicillin allergy label do harm?
options: The label can cause a real allergy
It makes the illness last longer
slides.explanation: Broader antibiotics also kill helpful gut bacteria and leave room for drug-resistant superbugs, which can spread to other people.
